identity.title: FlashVID: Efficient Video Large Language Models via Training-free Tree-based Spatiotemporal Token Merging

problem.claim: Video large language models process many visual tokens, creating substantial computational inefficiency.

gap.claim: Existing acceleration frameworks typically compress spatial and temporal redundancy separately, overlooking their relationships and potentially producing suboptimal spatiotemporal compression.

contributions.claim: The authors introduce FlashVID, a training-free inference-acceleration framework combining attention- and diversity-based token selection with tree-based spatiotemporal token merging.
The authors present FlashVID as a training-free, plug-and-play module for extending the number of video frames processed by VLLMs.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors distinguish FlashVID through joint, fine-grained spatiotemporal redundancy handling using ADTS followed by TSTM, without additional training.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report experiments on three representative VLLMs and five video-understanding benchmarks, describing the method as effective and generalizable.
The authors report that retaining 10% of visual tokens preserves 99.1% of LLaVA-OneVision's performance.
The authors report that FlashVID enables a 10× increase in video-frame input to Qwen2.5-VL and an 8.6% relative improvement under the same computational budget.

narrative_sequence.summary: VLLMs face computational inefficiency because video processing requires many visual tokens.
Separate spatial and temporal compression misses dynamic spatiotemporal relationships, while correlated features can shift in position, scale, or orientation over time.
FlashVID uses ADTS for representative-token selection and TSTM for fine-grained spatiotemporal redundancy elimination.
The authors report benchmark evidence, high retained performance at 10% token retention, and longer-frame processing within a fixed budget.

source_observation.claim: The abstract links a specific failure mode—independent spatial and temporal compression—to a method that jointly addresses spatiotemporal redundancy, then reports token-retention and fixed-budget outcomes.

lessons.interpretation: A strong abstract can align the method's design directly with the diagnosed limitation and quantify the resulting efficiency–performance tradeoff.
lessons.application: When proposing compression, define the overlooked dependency, make the mechanism target it explicitly, and report both retained quality and compute or input-scaling consequences.
lessons.exception: This framing is less suitable when the task has no meaningful cross-axis dependency or when quality and computational budgets cannot be measured comparably.

unknowns: The abstract names LLaVA-OneVision and Qwen2.5-VL but does not provide the complete roster of three evaluated VLLMs, the identities of the five benchmarks, baseline methods, or detailed evaluation protocols.
The conditions and metric underlying the reported 99.1% preservation and 8.6% relative improvement are not specified.
The abstract does not provide ablations separating ADTS from TSTM.

editorial_revisions.before: The abstract does not identify the three VLLMs, five benchmarks, baseline methods, or detailed evaluation protocols.
editorial_revisions.after: The abstract names LLaVA-OneVision and Qwen2.5-VL but does not provide the complete roster of three evaluated VLLMs, the identities of the five benchmarks, baseline methods, or detailed evaluation protocols.
